blocks.text: Producing quicklime (calcium oxide) from limestone (calcium carbonate) is one of the oldest and most basic industrial processes. Quicklime is vital in construction (cement, mortar), agriculture (soil treatment), metallurgy and many chemical industries. Limestone is an abundant sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate.

Limestone is heated in a lime kiln to about 900-1000 C, a thermal decomposition called calcination: CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g) on heating. In modern kilns the charge is heated by circulating hot gases. The reaction is reversible in a closed container, so carbon dioxide is removed continuously; this shifts the equilibrium to the right and gives a large amount of product.

blocks.alt: A cut-away stone lime kiln. Crushed limestone (CaCO3) is tipped from a cart into the top of the chimney (INPUT). In the burning zone, at 900-1000 C, a fuel burner enters from the left and coal and natural gas from the right. Below, CaO collects on a grate with arrows rising from beneath it, and CaO is carried out into a cart.
